lead: IP delivers a packet to a host. A host runs many programs, so the packet must still reach the right process. The transport layer adds a 16-bit port number to the IP address and uses that pair to hand data to the correct application. This is process-to-process delivery. It is why a phone can run a web browser, a DNS lookup and a video call at the same time. Ports appear whenever you type a URL, configure a firewall, or read that a service listens on port 443.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for layering and the TCP/IP suite, and Unit 4 for IPv4 addresses and datagram delivery.

sections.h3: From host delivery to process delivery

blocks.text: The network layer carries a datagram from one host to another host. Its address identifies an interface on a host. The transport layer goes one step further: it delivers data to a process, meaning a running program. To do that it uses port addressing and a socket address.

items: Segmentation and reassembly: split an application message into segments and put it back together.
Connection control: for TCP, open and close a connection; for UDP, no connection.

blocks.text: An IP address alone cannot name a process, because many processes share one host. A port number is a 16-bit unsigned integer, so it ranges from 0 to 65535. A socket address is an IP address plus a port number, written 192.0.2.10:80. Some syllabi call the port a TSAP, Transport Service Access Point, and call the IP-plus-port pair a socket.
The 16-bit port space is divided by convention, not by hardware. The ranges below are the standard assignment.

A client asking a server usually gets an ephemeral source port from its operating system. Ephemeral means short-lived; the port is freed after the connection closes. The server uses a well-known port such as 80 for HTTP or 53 for DNS. Registered ports are used by applications that need a stable number without being part of the standard set. The pair of IP address and port is the socket address.

A server has a listening socket on its well-known port. When a client connects, TCP creates a separate connection socket for that client. Both sockets can show port 80 at the server, but they are different sockets.

Multiplexing happens at the sender: the transport layer collects data from several processes, adds a port number to each segment, and passes the segments to IP. Demultiplexing happens at the receiver: the transport layer reads the port fields and delivers each segment to the right process. The lookup rule differs between UDP and TCP.

For a connectionless protocol such as UDP, demultiplexing uses the destination port. The receiving socket may be bound to a local IP address, but there is no per-connection four-tuple. A UDP server on port 53 receives all DNS queries addressed to that port and uses the source fields only if it needs to reply.

For connection-oriented TCP, demultiplexing uses the four-tuple: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. Two browsers on one client talking to one web server have the same server IP and port. Only the client source port separates their connections. A server that demultiplexed by destination port alone would mix the two connections. The four-tuple also identifies the connection during connection setup and release.

spec.aria: A client host with two browsers on source ports 52000 and 52001 sending to the server 192.0.2.10 port 80, which hands each segment to its own socket, with the two four-tuples written below.

examples.question: A web server at 192.0.2.10:80 is serving two browsers on the same client host 203.0.113.7, using source ports 52000 and 52001. Write the four-tuple the server transport layer uses to demultiplex each arriving segment, and say why the pair (192.0.2.10, 80) is the same for both.
steps: Client host: IP 203.0.113.7. First browser source port: 52000.
Four-tuple order is source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. Connection 1: (203.0.113.7, 52000, 192.0.2.10, 80).
Both segments have destination IP 192.0.2.10 and destination port 80 because they go to the same server service. The source port differs, so TCP treats them as two connections.
examples.answer: Connection 1 is (203.0.113.7, 52000, 192.0.2.10, 80) and connection 2 is (203.0.113.7, 52001, 192.0.2.10, 80); the shared server socket address means the source port separates the two connections.

sports = [52000, 52001]
dport = 80
for sp in sports:
    print(sp)
print(dport)

traps: Demultiplexing TCP by destination port alone; two clients of one server then look like one connection.
Calling port 80 the connection; it is only one field. The TCP connection is the four-tuple.
Mixing up multiplexing at the sender with demultiplexing at the receiver.
Forgetting that a port is 16 bits: 0 to 65535, not 0 to 65536.
Treating the listening socket as the connection socket; accept creates a new socket per client.

quiz.q: What is a port number and how many bits does it use?
quiz.a: A port number identifies a process on a host. It is a 16-bit unsigned integer, range 0 to 65535.

quiz.q: Name the three standard port ranges.
Why is an IP address alone not enough for process-to-process delivery?
quiz.a: Many processes share one host IP address. The port number selects the receiving process, so IP plus port gives the socket address.

quiz.q: A server is at 198.51.100.5:443. A client at 203.0.113.9 uses source ports 61000 and 61001. Write the two TCP four-tuples at the server.
quiz.a: (203.0.113.9, 61000, 198.51.100.5, 443) and (203.0.113.9, 61001, 198.51.100.5, 443). The server IP and port are shared; the client source ports differ.

quiz.q: Why does a TCP server fail to separate two clients if it demultiplexes by destination port only?
quiz.a: Both clients send to the same server IP and port, so the destination port matches both. The source IP and source port are needed to tell the two connections apart; they are part of the four-tuple.

quiz.q: Distinguish a listening socket from a connection socket at a TCP server.
quiz.a: The listening socket waits on the well-known port for new connection requests. The connection socket is created for one accepted client and carries that connection data; both may show the same server port.

quiz.q: A UDP server on port 53 gets two datagrams from different client ports. Does UDP demultiplex them into two separate server sockets automatically?
quiz.a: No. UDP demultiplexing uses the destination port, so both datagrams go to the same UDP socket. The application can read the source fields to reply, but it does not get two connection sockets.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real systems, the port space is a security boundary: firewalls filter by port, and port scanning finds open services. Modern kernels use hash tables for four-tuple lookup, so demultiplexing cost stays near constant as connections grow. QUIC carries streams over UDP and uses connection IDs rather than the four-tuple, which lets a connection survive an IP address change. Search for TCP socket lookup, ephemeral port exhaustion, or QUIC connection ID to go further.
